title: Things that can get in the bin.
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien lists education terms and habits that he believes do more harm than good despite good intentions, framed as a counterpoint to an earlier post about positive impact. His targets include differentiation as a catch-all that can lower expectations, the phrase the explicit teaching portion of the lesson, which he says turns explicit teaching into a cliff of release, rigid instructional models, a diluted zone of proximal development, productive struggle for novices, autonomy used to resist consistency, Bloom's and Maslow's hierarchies, the teacher-centred versus student-centred split, flipped classrooms and in-class note taking. His recurring argument is that well taught explicit lessons cycle through gradual release and responsive checks, keeping the teacher constantly active and the students interactive. He proposes principles over rigid lesson models, bounded autonomy and knowledge before desirable difficulty. The final entries turn to named organisations and individuals, which is a more personal and polemical register than the pedagogy sections.
points: Differentiate by support, not by content, and prefer the clearer term responsive teaching.
Explicit teaching is a continuous cycle of gradual release and checking, not a talky stage followed by independent work.
Instructional principles with teacher judgement beat rigid lesson models that penalise a teacher for correcting a misconception.
Novices need knowledge before struggle, so productive struggle without it widens gaps; desirable difficulties come after knowledge is secure.
Autonomy works best as bounded autonomy in how a shared resource or method is brought to life.
quotes: The key problem is that some of these scenarios are lowering the expectations for students, but in a way that sounds like the teacher is doing a great job.

We shouldn’t be differentiating by content, because students should have the same high expectations of outcome. Differentiating by support is great, but that’s why the phrase ‘responsive teaching’ is so much clearer in that space.

This phrase upsets me to such a significant degree because it undermines the whole idea of explicit teaching and our gradual release of responsibility. Instead it creates an idea of a sheer cliff of release where the teacher talks and then magically the students should be able to work independently.
A truly well done explicitly taught lesson is high effort from the teacher as they are ‘on’ basically the whole time.
The mutation of instructional models tends to come when school leaders have an expectation that a certain element will be occurring at a certain time in the lesson.
Novices are not little experts. Presenting students with an unfamiliar problem without first teaching them they required knowledge to complete it is absurd.

Autonomy is actually incredibly important, yet the way the word has been weaponised in education as a comeback against anything that requires consistency or low-variance is frustrating. A better term would likely be bounded autonomy.

The idea that explicit teaching is teacher centred and inquiry learning is student centred frustrates me to no end. It poses explicit teaching as a mode of instruction where the teacher just talks ad nauseum without any student interaction.
